<objective>
Complete the task surface the tracer opened: list, event history, cancellation, model routing, and the
cap resolution order — over HTTP and over the CLI, in 1:1 parity.

Purpose: the tracer proved one task can be created and observed. TASK-02, TASK-04, TASK-06, and SAFE-03
are the rest of what makes the surface usable — and cancellation in particular is the one operation that
must not grow a second teardown path, because D-26 explicitly routes a cancelled task down the same
archival sequence as any other terminal task.

Output: `fleet task create|list|show|cancel` and their four routes, with model and cap resolution
implemented and asserted at every level of the resolution order.
</objective>

  <behavior>
    - `resolveModel({ task: 'opus', fleetYml: 'haiku', config: 'sonnet' })` returns `opus`; omitting the task value returns `haiku`; omitting both returns `sonnet`; omitting all three returns `sonnet`.
    - `resolveModel({ task: 'cheap' })` returns `haiku`, `'default'` returns `sonnet`, `'high'` returns `opus` — the tier names are translated before the value is stored.
    - A model value that is neither one of the three aliases nor one of the three tier names is rejected at task creation with a 400, naming the accepted values.
    - A full dated model id such as `claude-haiku-4-5` is rejected at task creation, because a pinned id silently rots across model releases while an alias does not.
    - The resolved allowed-tools and disallowed-tools lists follow the same precedence: a `.fleet.yml` override replaces the default list wholesale rather than merging into it.
    - `resolveCaps` and `resolveModel` produce the same precedence given equivalent inputs — asserted by a shared `it.each` table exercising all four precedence levels for each.
  </behavior>
  <action>
Add `resolveModel(input)` to `src/tasks/service.ts` implementing D-12's precedence: task value, then
`.fleet.yml`, then Fleet config, then the `sonnet` column default. Store and pass the CLI ALIAS
(`haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`), never a full dated model id — an alias survives model releases while a
pinned id silently rots, which is the whole reason D-12 chose aliases. Reject a dated id at the
validation boundary with a message naming the three accepted aliases, so a user who pins one gets a clear
error instead of a session that runs on the wrong model.

Add the three tier names as CLI-surface sugar: `cheap` maps to `haiku`, `default` to `sonnet`, `high` to
`opus`. Translate at the validation boundary so a tier name is never persisted — the database holds an
alias or nothing.

**Check `02-03-SUMMARY.md` before implementing.** Plan 02-03's model-alias probe determines whether the
installed CLI accepts bare aliases at all. If the recorded result says it does, pass the alias straight
through to `--model`. If the recorded result says it requires a full dated name, do NOT silently
hardcode one: implement a single named `ALIAS_TO_MODEL_ID` lookup, document that it must be revisited on
every CLI upgrade, and record that in the plan summary — a lookup table introduces exactly the rot D-12
was avoiding, so it must be visible rather than buried.

Add the per-project override keys to `fleetYmlSchema` in `src/registry/fleet-yaml.ts`: optional `model`,
`max_turns`, `wall_clock_cap_ms`, `allowed_tools`, and `disallowed_tools`. Because that schema is
`.strict()`, adding the keys is precisely what turns them from "unrecognised key" warnings into genuine
overrides. Do not relax `.strict()` — the warning behavior for genuinely unknown keys is the feature.
This plan is the sole owner of `src/registry/fleet-yaml.ts` in wave 3.

An override of `allowed_tools` or `disallowed_tools` REPLACES the default list wholesale rather than
merging: a merge would make it impossible for a project to narrow the default set, and narrowing is the
main reason a project would override at all.

Extend `src/tasks/service.test.ts` with a shared `it.each` precedence table exercising all four levels
for the model, the two caps, and the two tool lists, plus the rejection cases.
  </action>

  <behavior>
    - `GET /tasks` returns every task ordered newest-first, and accepts an optional `status` query filter and an optional `projectId` filter; an unknown status value fails zod validation with a 400.
    - `GET /tasks` on an empty database returns `{ tasks: [] }` with a 200, not a 404.
    - `GET /tasks/:id/events` returns the task's `events` rows in ascending `id` order, including rows with `accepted: 0`, because a rejected transition is a queryable fact rather than a hidden one.
    - `GET /tasks/:id/events` for an unknown task id returns 404 `task_not_found`, not an empty array.
    - `POST /tasks/:id/cancel` on a `running` task returns 200, kills the process group, records a `CANCEL` event with source `user`, and leaves the task in `failed`.
    - `POST /tasks/:id/cancel` on a `queued` task removes it from the queue and records `CANCEL`; on an already-terminal task it returns 409 `task_not_running`.
    - `POST /tasks/:id/cancel` accepts a `.strict()` empty body — an unrecognised key in the body fails validation rather than being silently ignored.
    - After cancellation the worktree is archived by the same `archiveWorktree()` call any other terminal task uses, with dirty work captured first.
  </behavior>
  <action>
Extend `src/api/http/routes/tasks.ts` with three routes, mirroring `projects.ts`'s shape exactly:
`app.withTypeProvider&lt;ZodTypeProvider&gt;()`, a zod schema on every body, querystring, and params, and
typed errors thrown from the service layer rather than caught and rendered inline.

`GET /tasks` — a `listTasksQuery` zod schema with optional `status` (a `z.enum` over `TASK_STATES`, so an
unknown value is a validation failure rather than an empty result) and optional `projectId`. Returns
`{ tasks }`.

`GET /tasks/:id/events` — reuses the existing `getTaskEvents(db, taskId)` from
`src/core/event-store/record-event.ts`. Do NOT write a second query: that function already orders by
ascending `id` rather than `created_at`, deliberately, because two events written in the same millisecond
share a timestamp string while the autoincrement id is strictly monotonic — and that same id is Phase 5's
SSE `Last-Event-ID`. Include rejected rows (`accepted: 0`): a rejected transition is a queryable fact,
and hiding it would make the exact class of bug the `RATE_LIMITED` gap represented invisible.

`POST /tasks/:id/cancel` — a `.strict()` empty-object body schema, so an unrecognised key fails
validation. Delegates to `cancelTask(db, scheduler, runner, id)` in `src/tasks/service.ts`, which:
looks up the task; returns `TaskServiceError('task_not_running')` if its status is not `queued` or
`running`; for a `running` task calls `runner.kill(task)` (which does the process-group teardown) and
then `recordEvent(db, id, { type: 'CANCEL' }, 'user')`; for a `queued` task removes it from the
scheduler's pending set and records the same event. Then — and this is D-26's whole point — lets the
STANDARD terminal-state handler archive the worktree. There must be no cancellation-specific teardown
branch: cancelled work is inspectable exactly like any other terminal task's, and a second teardown path
is a second thing to keep correct. Assert this structurally in the test by checking that the archival
call site reached during cancellation is the same one reached on a normal completion.

Create `src/api/http/routes/tasks.test.ts` using `parity.test.ts`'s live-daemon harness shape
(`mkdtempSync` for the DB dir, `openDatabase`, `runMigrations`, `buildApp`, `app.inject`, `afterEach`
teardown with `rmSync(..., { recursive: true, force: true })`). Also assert route registration the way
`parity.test.ts` does, via `app.hasRoute({ method, url })` for all five task routes.
  </action>

  </verify>

    - A test cancels a running fixture-backed task and asserts a `CANCEL` events row exists with `source === 'user'` and `accepted === 1`, and that `tasks.status` is `failed`.
    - A test asserts cancelling an already-`failed` task returns 409 with `error.code === 'task_not_running'`.
    - A test asserts `POST /tasks/:id/cancel` with body `{ force: true }` returns 400 (strict body).
    - A test asserts the worktree directory no longer exists and the task branch still exists after cancellation.
    - `app.hasRoute` returns `true` for all five task routes.
    - `src/api/http/errors.ts` is unchanged by this plan.
    - `npm test` (whole `unit` project) exits 0.
  </acceptance_criteria>
  <done>The HTTP task surface is complete, and a cancelled task walks the identical terminal path as any other finished task.</done>
